title: When the Well Falls
premise: Theo Ravensworth, a property surveyor, is sent to appraise Hollowell House, a derelict farmhouse whose previous owner vanished in 1974 along with a child who was never found. As Theo documents the rooms, the house begins documenting him back: measurements change, his sleep recordings capture a second voice answering questions he never asked aloud, and his own memories start arriving from someone else's childhood. He learns the house sustains itself on what it takes — and in 1974 its keeper took a child to feed it. To survive, Theo must return what was taken, but the house will accept only an equivalent: something loved, freely given. In the end Theo gives the house his memory of the person he loves most, walking out alive but unable to remember why he came or who waits for him at home.
about_author: Juniper Ashgrove is the pen name of a former rural land assessor who spent a decade cataloguing abandoned properties across the English countryside. Their debut novel draws on field notes from houses that were demolished before anyone could ask too many questions.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Third-person limited POV following Theo as he arrives at Hollowell House for a routine estate appraisal, finding the interior oddly preserved despite decades of abandonment. His instruments give impossible readings — rooms larger inside than out. The emotional beat is professional unease curdling into fascination; Theo, recently divorced and hollowed out, feels the house noticing him.

chapters.title: Explanations
chapters.summary: Still Theo's POV. He spends the night in the house to finish measurements, rationalizing every sound: settling timber, wind in the flue, mice in the walls. He finds a child's shoe behind a sealed hearth and pockets it without deciding to. The beat is self-deception — five years of practiced denial deployed against evidence that refuses to fit.

chapters.title: What the Recorder Heard
chapters.summary: Theo reviews his overnight audio log and hears a second voice — dry, patient, answering questions in the pauses between his own breathing. The questions are about him: whether he is alone, whether anyone would come looking. The beat shifts from unease to dread; the denial that served him for five years collapses in eleven minutes of playback.

chapters.title: The Ravensworth Noises
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter in Theo's POV, revealing the noises began five years ago in his own flat after his marriage ended — meaning the house has been with him far longer than this assignment. The beat is vertigo: the story's timeline inverts, and Theo realizes he wasn't drawn to Hollowell House; he was returned to it.

POV shifts to Edith Marlowe, the house's last owner, in diary fragments and a final tape recording. She describes her bargain: the house kept her dying husband alive in exchange for 'a tithe,' and when she refused to pay it again, it took her grandson instead. The beat is guilt fossilized into ritual; Edith's record-keeping becomes Theo's map.

chapters.title: The Tithe
chapters.summary: Back in Theo's POV, he deciphers Edith's notes: the house runs on memory, and the missing child, Samuel, exists inside it still — awake, aware, kept as fuel. The second voice belongs to Samuel. The beat is horrified compassion; Theo understands the house doesn't kill, it keeps, and being kept is worse.

chapters.title: Rooms That Remember
chapters.summary: Theo enters the house's interior spaces, where walls show him other people's memories — including his own ex-wife's, which the house has been harvesting through him for years. The beat is violation and grief; he sees how much of his life has already been eaten, and how little he noticed going hungry.

chapters.title: Negotiation
chapters.summary: Theo attempts to bargain with the house directly, offering the shoe, Edith's tapes, anything material. The house refuses: it accepts only what is loved and freely given. The second voice warns him not to pay, that freedom inside the dark is better than emptiness outside it. The beat is moral crisis — survival now requires choosing what to lose.

chapters.title: The Return
chapters.summary: Climax. Theo carries Samuel's shoe to the sealed hearth and offers himself as the tithe instead, demanding the boy's release. The house begins taking everything — his name, his history, his face — until Theo, at the threshold of erasure, chooses the one thing left: his love for his ex-wife, given freely. The house takes it and lets them both go. The beat is sacrifice at the exact price demanded.

chapters.title: Appraised
chapters.summary: Resolution in Theo's POV, fragmented and calm. He signs the appraisal, drives home past a woman he feels he should know, and files the report on a house he cannot remember entering. The final image: his sleep recorder running all night, silent — except once, faintly, a child laughing. The beat is bittersweet peace; survival was purchased, and the invoice arrives slowly, forever.
